title: The Crisis of the Tax State Revisited: Artificial Intelligence, Business Conflict, and Digital Fiscal Capacity
abstract: Rich democracies finance the modern state through labour taxation. If artificial intelligence (AI) reduces the labour share, governments will have to replace lost revenue, especially through consumption or capital taxation. AI rents arise from intangible assets with hard-to-observe transaction prices. Taxing them requires digital fiscal capacity, the legal and administrative resources for identifying and valuing AI returns and distinguishing rents from normal returns. In its absence, blunt capital taxation disproportionately burdens conventional, non-AI firms. With digital fiscal capacity, targeted taxation becomes possible and shifts part of the burden to AI firms, making conventional firms pivotal in the conflict between voters favouring such taxation and AI firms opposing it. Our model examines investment in this capacity as the transition to an AI economy empowers AI firms politically. Declining revenue from labour taxation and greater inequality strengthen conventional firms’ support; their fiscal stakes, the speed of transition, and political power relative to AI firms determine whether and when investment occurs. The extent to which technological change transforms the tax state thus depends crucially on intra-business conflict over the incidence of capital taxation.
series_note: Working papers are circulated for discussion and comment; they have not been peer reviewed. Views expressed are those of the authors.
